USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should consolidate the May 19 truce by staying in active negotiation rather than escalating or unilaterally conceding. Keep the threatened Section 301 tariffs on hold as leverage while our Commerce/Ross mission to Beijing secures hard, verifiable purchase commitments (agriculture, energy, autos, soybeans) from the vague joint statement, and avoid capitulating on ZTE — that concession is domestically toxic to a bipartisan Congress and weakens our negotiation position. Maintain a firm line on the unresolved structural issues (forced technology transfer, cyber theft) so the truce is converted into enforceable deliverables rather than a facade.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to U.S. interests right now is modest and net-negative: the timeline shows China conceded ground (May 19 joint statement committing to 'significantly increase' purchases, per the event_timeline), and it followed up with concrete gestures — cutting auto tariffs 25% to 15% and dropping the sorghum anti-dumping probe (CSMonitor, 5/23). Macro conditions support our leverage: IP is rising, the 10-year yield is ~3.0%, the broad dollar is up to ~111.7, and consumer sentiment ~98 — the U.S. is strong, not threatened (country_health USA). Markets rallied on the truce (Dow +300, Politico 5/21). This sits at the low/opportunity end of the scale (~-0.25), not existential. That underpins the mildly de-escalatory action stance: escalating now would break a truce we already won and spook markets, while full concession would forfeit the unresolved structural tech/IP gains Lighthizer explicitly flagged as unmet and would reward what a bipartisan Congress (Senate Banking Committee bill) is already rejecting as weakness on ZTE. Instead we 'hold' tariff fire and negotiate to lock in China's purchase commitments under the credible threat Mnuchin articulated — that we can put tariffs back on if China fails to deliver. Fragility (vague, non-binding deal; China halting soybean purchases as a warning) argues for caution and verification, not overreach.

Markets rallied (Dow +300) on the truce; IP rising, 10Y ~3.0%, dollar ~111.7 — US economy strong
Structural tech/IP issues (forced transfer, cyber theft) remain unresolved per Lighthizer
Congressional bipartisan rebuke of easing the ZTE ban signals domestic limits on concessions
China's conciliatory gestures: auto tariff cut 25%→15%, dropped sorghum anti-dumping
Truce fragile and vague: no binding figures; China halted soybean purchases as warning shot

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should consolidate the pause won in the May 19 joint statement — hold the current de-escalatory posture, follow through on the pledge to significantly increase purchases of US agriculture and energy, and deploy talks to press for ZTE relief and the shelving of the Section 301 tariff list — while refusing structural concessions on forced-technology-transfer and industrial policy. This is the moment to bank the 'trade war on hold' outcome and convert it into durable de-escalation, not to escalate.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but contained, so I read it at +0.35. On the threat side, the US proposed a Section 301 tariff list covering ~$50B of Chinese aerospace/ICT/robotics lines (event timeline 2018-04-03) and imposed a denial order banning ZTE from US components (2018-04-16) — genuine firm-level and sectoral targeting aimed at China's tech ambitions. Yet the trajectory since mid-May is de-escalation: the May 19 joint statement had both sides agree not to impose new tariffs while talks continue and Mnuchin explicitly said the trade war is 'on hold' (web_search: CNN/Politico). China secured this pause without committing to the $200B purchase figure, and even gained a softer US line on ZTE. Critically, the dispute is not yet biting the real economy — China Q1 exports rose 7.4% y/y and GDP grew 6.8% (web_search: Reuters/China Internet Watch), so there is no domestic urgency forcing escalation. On the action side, escalating now would be self-defeating: it would hand the US hawks (Lighthizer keeps tariffs 'in reserve') the trigger they want and unwind the pause that already favors China. Over-conceding on structural IP/tech-transfer demands would be politically and strategically costly. The disciplined move is negotiate — honor the purchase pledge to lock in the pause, seek tariff rollback and ZTE relief, and give away nothing structural yet.
